nature-mkt-026.q: What share of cancer drugs are natural or inspired by nature?
nature-mkt-026.a: 70% of all cancer drugs are natural or bioinspired products, and over 40% of medicines come from nature.

nature-mkt-028.q: Why do criminal and terrorist groups take part in wildlife trafficking?
nature-mkt-028.a: They use trafficking to raise money; other demand comes from culture, such as bushmeat and traditional medicine.

nature-mkt-054.q: How can a land trust protect land without owning it outright?
nature-mkt-054.a: It can buy an easement or development, mining or logging rights while the land stays private.

nature-mkt-016.q: Where do these extra costs bite hardest?
nature-mkt-016.a: Where projects are small, varied or need a lot of monitoring and checking; the costs can make projects less attractive to investors.

nature-mkt-040.q: Which report brought the term ESG to prominence?

nature-mkt-042.q: What did Milton Friedman argue about social responsibility?
nature-mkt-042.a: That it harms a firm's financial performance.

nature-mkt-021.q: How well do disclosure rules work when they stay voluntary?
nature-mkt-021.a: Research shows they have limited effect.

nature-mkt-048.q: Why do green bonds tend to pay lower yields than ordinary bonds?
nature-mkt-048.a: Because high demand for them pushes their yields down, as studies find.

nature-mkt-061.q: How do these bonds differ from ordinary bonds?
nature-mkt-061.a: They have no fixed return; what they pay depends on social outcomes.

nature-mkt-010.q: What problem were these projects introduced to fix?
nature-mkt-010.a: WWF brought them in during the mid-1980s to fix the problems of the 'fines and fences' approach, which left local people out.

nature-mkt-004.q: Which solutions to human-wildlife conflict tend to work best?
nature-mkt-004.a: Those that involve local communities in planning, carrying out and maintaining them.

nature-res-204.q: Why do scarcer resources become more valuable?
nature-res-204.a: Value depends on how much exists in nature and how costly it is to extract; under supply and demand, scarcity raises value.

nature-res-220.q: When did resource extraction reach an industrial scale?
nature-res-220.a: In the 19th century, as mining, steam power and machinery pushed extraction far beyond earlier levels.

nature-res-244.q: Why does sustainable yield apply only to renewable resources?
nature-res-244.a: Because taking non-renewable resources always shrinks natural capital.

nature-res-221.q: Under efficient extraction, how fast does a resource's net price rise?
nature-res-221.a: Each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate.

nature-res-245.q: How does the World Bank describe the blue economy?
nature-res-245.a: As sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while keeping ocean ecosystems healthy.

nature-res-242.q: In the famous bet, what did Simon expect raw material prices to do?
nature-res-242.a: Not rise in the long run, while Ehrlich expected population growth to outstrip resources.

nature-res-238.q: What makes material in the Earth's crust a mineral resource?
nature-res-238.a: It has reasonable prospects of eventually being extracted at a profit.

nature-res-224.q: How likely to be produced are proven (1P) reserves?

nature-res-202.q: Which book popularised the idea of petro-aggression?
nature-res-202.a: Jeff Colgan's 2013 book, which found petrostates far more likely to start international conflicts.

nature-res-216.q: What is the classic example of a resource nobody needs any more?
nature-res-216.a: Arrowhead-grade flint, since sharpened scrap steel is simpler.

nature-res-230.q: In the resource movement effect, what does a boom do to workers?
nature-res-230.a: It pulls them into the booming sector, called direct deindustrialisation.

nature-res-228.q: Is there an agreed definition of a critical raw material?
nature-res-228.a: No; criticality varies with time, country and context.

nature-res-033.q: How does the FAO define a fishery?
nature-res-033.a: As an activity leading to harvesting fish, whether caught wild or farmed.

nature-res-001.q: When do wild fish stocks count as renewable?
nature-res-001.a: When they produce a yearly surplus that careful management can harvest without lowering future productivity.

nature-res-080.q: Which fields does marine conservation draw on?
nature-res-080.a: Marine biology, ecology, oceanography and fisheries science, plus economics, maritime law and policy.

nature-res-057.q: What mainly causes illegal and unreported fishing?
nature-res-057.a: Failure to enforce existing laws, often rooted in poor national governance.

nature-res-028.a: Depleting the spawning adults until too few remain to replenish the stock.

nature-res-066.q: What is the most common form of recreational fishing?
nature-res-066.a: Angling with rod, reel, line, hooks and bait.

nature-res-082.q: What does the treaty's Multilateral System provide?
nature-res-082.a: Free access to 64 of the world's most important crops for research, breeding and training.

nature-res-015.q: Why do many conservation biologists distrust maximum sustainable yield?
nature-res-015.a: They see it as dangerous and misused, and blame it for the collapse of many fisheries.

nature-res-006.q: How did NOAA honour this tool in 2007?
nature-res-006.a: It named it one of the ten biggest scientific breakthroughs in its 200-year history.

nature-res-012.q: Why was the United States Fish Commission set up?
nature-res-012.a: To find out why New England fisheries were declining.

nature-res-065.q: In the simplest growth model, what is a fish's growth in length proportional to?
nature-res-065.a: The gap between its current length and its ultimate length.

nature-res-042.q: How does a turtle excluder device work?
nature-res-042.a: A grid deflects turtles out of the trawl net through an opening.

nature-res-011.q: Which parts of the sea floor have been trawled repeatedly?
nature-res-011.a: Nearly all continental shelves and large areas of slopes, ridges and seamounts.

nature-res-029.q: What does economic overfishing add to the judgement?
nature-res-029.a: The cost of fishing, making the fishery less profitable than it could be.

nature-res-076.q: Who launched the first seafood certification program?

nature-res-070.q: Where do fisheries data come from?
nature-res-070.a: From the fishery itself, such as recorded landings, and from independent surveys using nets or acoustic and video methods.

nature-res-063.q: Why is virtual population analysis called 'virtual'?
nature-res-063.a: Population size is never measured directly but worked backwards from catches and an assumed natural death rate.

nature-res-020.q: How do catch shares change fishers' lives?
nature-res-020.a: They can schedule trips as they like, boom-and-bust cycles fade, and fishing in dangerous weather becomes unnecessary.

nature-res-085.q: How do you get the equilibrium catch for a level of fishing effort?
nature-res-085.a: Set the catch equal to the stock's natural growth.

nature-res-107.q: Into which categories does the IPCC group land?
nature-res-107.a: Forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands.

nature-res-088.q: If the world has enough fresh water, where does scarcity come from?
nature-res-088.a: A mismatch between when and where people need water and when and where it is available.

nature-res-169.q: What do people with high water security have?
nature-res-169.a: Always enough water of acceptable quality for health, livelihoods and production.

nature-res-123.q: At which stage does most food waste arise?

nature-res-160.q: In slash-and-burn farming, why do farmers eventually move on?
nature-res-160.a: After a few years nutrients run down and weeds and pests invade.

nature-res-174.q: Which products do non-wood forest products leave out?

nature-res-093.q: Which three pillars must sustainable forest management balance?

nature-res-151.q: How is prior appropriation often summed up?
nature-res-151.a: 'First in time, first in right': later users take only what is left without harming earlier ones.
